General News 
NBC Switch 
Continued from page 1 
format on the air almost one year to 
a contemporary easy listening play - 
list aimed at listeners in the 25 to 49 
age group. 
The changes are the brainchild or 
John Lund, program director of 
both the AM and FM stations, and 
are calculated to fdl what Lund sees 
as "a void in radio programming in 
this city." 
Lund stops short of calling the 
new formats "nostalgia radio," but 
stresses that the listeners in the age 
groupings to which his stations are 
catering have a psychological need 
to return-if only through music- 
"to the best years of their life." 
Lund who moved to NBC from 
WNEW -AM just two months ago, 
accuses most New York radio sta- 
tions of being boring, predictable. 
confining and redundant. He says 
"Our research has shown that 
people want radio to give them the 
life they don't have. It is largely a 
psychological need and we think we 
can fill it" 
Lund emphasizes that the trou- 
bled AM station will not be just an- 
other `jukebox MOR" station, but 
-II ha e 
e contemporary playlist 
that will mù the golden years of rock 
'n' roll -Elvis Presley and the 
Beatles -with current MOR sounds. 
The station thus retains several of 
the top rack names it has been airing 
for the past three years. 
Lund explains that he wants to 
reach those people who were teen- 
agers in rock's heyday, but who are 
now a little older and a little more 
sophisticated and not into the acid 
rock music of the Top 40s playlisls. 
He adds. "The audience we are 
trying to reach are the young house- 
wives and the blue collar worker 
who lighten their work day by listen- 
ing to their transistor radios." 
The NBC program director also 
feels that the audience for today's 
rack sounds is shrinking, and that 
this is the opportune time for 
change. He feels that this theory is 
borne out by what he calls the over- 
whelming positive public response 
to the station's new time slot of IO 
a.m. to 2 p.m. for the popular 
"Cousin" Bence Morrow. 
Lund reasons that Morrow, who 
has been a Top 40 radio institution 
in New York for the past 15 years. 
can relate to the new audience 
WNBC -AM is now trying to reach.

Theater Bid 
LOS ANGELES -The city Recrc- 
ation Board has turned down bids 
offering large advances from four 
rock- oriented promoters to operate 
municipally -owned 3,500-seat out- 
doors Greek Theater in Griffith 
Park during the summer of 1975. 
Continuing to run the Greek will 
be James Doolittle's Greek Theater 
Assn., which has a total deficit of 
some $1.5 million since taking over 
the theater in 1952. The GTA has 
booked Greek Theater largely with 
touring cultural attractions such as 
ballet and drama troupes. It will get 
a 1975 subsidy of $60,000 from Los 
Angeles County. 
The city board recommended that 
Mayar Bradley appoint a committee 
representing both government and 
the entertainment industry to study 
long -range goals for the Greek. 
GTA's most serious competition 
for the 1975 license was apparently 
New York -based Nederlander Pro- 
ductions, which operates a national 
chain of suburban concert theaters, 
such as the Pine Knob outside De- 
troit. Nederlander offered the city 
$50,000 in advance against 4 percent 
of the gross. 
The deal was rejected on the 
p grounds that a change from the cur - 
% rent non -profit corporation tax situ- 
p ation at the Greek would cut down 
on potential profits. Also the city 
was not yet ready to move the Greek 
en 
season into moneymaking popular 
"s entertainment, thus ending a tradi- 
m 
h onal policy of holding the Greek 
7 primarily for cultural attractions.

A 'Doubleheader' 
PHILADELPHIA -Just 
Jazz, 
center city showplace for name jazz 
talent, has become a "double- 
header" operation. 
The ground floor level has been 
renamed Cabaret at Just Jazz with 
"El Grande de Coca Cola" in for a 
limited engagement. The Cabaret 
floor will operate Tuesdays through 
Sundays, with two shows on Friday 
and Saturday nights. 
The second floor, where the jazz 
greats now hold forth, is known as 
Upstairs at Just Jazz, operating 
Monday through Saturday nights. 
Buddy Rich Six ushered in the 
doubleheader setup Monday (9). 
According to co-owner Al Schmidt, 
the Cabaret floor will bring in self- 
contained intimate revues or shows, 
while jan instrumentalists and sing- 
ers will hold forth upstairs.

SAN FRANCISCO -"The Song 
Of Crazy Horse" by new Fantasy 
artist J.D. Blackfoot has gained 
strong and immediate acceptance in 
the St. Louis area due in large part to 
the efforts of KSHE and disk jockey 
Shelley Graffman. 
The highly -localized 
grassroots 
response was strong enough for 
KSHE and promoter Ron Powell to 
draw 4,000 to two hastily- arranged 
Blackfoot performances at the Am- 
bassador Theater. 
Graffman recalls that the St. 
Louis affection for Blackfoot dates 
back to an LP he cut in 1970 for 
Mercury, "The Ultimate Prophecy."

Nader Sees Big 
Year For Rock 
ATLANTIC CITY -In spite of in- 
creasing hazards for the rock concert 
promoter, Richard Nader, who 
staged the three -day July Fourth 
weekend rock festival in the resort's 
Convention Hall last summer, paints 
an optimistic picture for the rock 
concertgoers in the new year. 
"Artists just won't be able to de- 
mand the huge salaries some of them 
have been demanding and ticket 
prices will come down," says Nader, 
whose rock 'n roll revival promo- 
bons have been highly successful in 
recent years. "And when salaries 
come down, the consumer will ben- 
efit." 
He admits, however, that one of 
the reasons for his recent successes at 
New York's Madison Square Gar- 
den promotions was the fact that he 
upped ticket prices. Cost of the top 
ticket went up to $8.50, a dollar more 
than what he had been charging. 
Even with the increased ticket 
price, Nader says he went home with 
less money than some of the prior 
shows because "the expenses today 
are much greater, there are larger 
costs for facilities and labor, and you 
have to pay so much more exten- 
sively for talent"

Edgar Winter: Once 
Too Shy To Make It 
By NAT FREEDLAND 
LOS ANGELES -Although Ed- 
gar Winter toured arenas in 69 cities 
from late spring to early autumn this 
year, grossing more than $4 million 
along the route, he claims he held 
himself back for years by shyness 
and lack of commercial ambition. 
While Edgar's four -year -older 
brother, virtuoso rock -blues guitarist 
Johnny Winter, reveled in the flash 
and showmanship of his role as 
leader of the hottest teenage rock 
band around their south Texas 
hometown of Beaumont, Edgar pre- 
ferred to stay in the background on 
his keyboards and saxophone as he 
provided much of the organizing 
force holding the group together. 
And every once in a while- Edgar 
would decide he could no longer 
stomach the "commercial sellout" of 
rock and go off to form ajazz group 
that struggled vainly to obtain 
enough Texas lounge bookings to 
stay alive. 
Even when Johnny won an un- 
precedented 
$600,000 
new- artist 
contract with Columbia Records 
and began to tour nationally, Edgar 
joined the road band but wore suits, 
ties and short hair onstage. He didn't 
want to distract audiences from the 
music by being the second wild - 
looking albino brother in the group. 
Edgar got a solo number at each 
concert, however, generally his high-

feel young customers are cherry - 
picking. 
Like many others, such as Biehn 
and the four -store Record Guild of 
America chain in Cleveland, Arnold 
stresses the gift theme in all his ad- 
vertising. 
Again, Arnold is representative. 
He reports 80 percent of his ad 
budget or more went into radio this 
holiday. Arnold hopes labels have 
saved some goodies for release after 
the holiday. 
Biehn says he expects to use more 
co-op dollars after the holidays than 
before. "We want to get that new 
component buyer into the store and 
make him a steady." 
Max Silverman of the I3 -store 
Washington, D.C., Waste Maxie 
string claims he's up 20 percent. 
Larry Davis of Abner, Colorado, 
feels he's up 15 percent for his 18 
stores. He says crash discounting, as 
low as $2.99 for 06.96 LPs, has 
gouged into his profits. 
Nashville retailers are holding 
their own or are up a bit. The Ernest 
Tubb Record Shop, Music Mart, 
Nicholson's High Fidelity Center 
and Dee's report about even. 
Harding Mall Shop reports a gen- 
eral increase. 
Tom Seaman, director of mer- 
chandising for the 70 -store Discount 
Records chain, reports sales slightly 
ahead of last year. Abby Levin, who 
runs mail -order for the chain, says 
he's 20 percent ahead. 
Seaman says the stores have been 
undergoing much internal change 
during this period, including inven- 
tory reduction and tightening, which 
might have had an effect Like most 
queried, he reports accessories doing 
very well, especially blank tape. 
Most Nashville retailers report 
they are handling between three and 
four different brands where they 
had one or two a year ago. Dis- 
counted multi -pabs lead the tape pa- 
rade. 
"We're doing very well," John 
Cohen, boss of the 40 -store Disc 
Records, reports. He says he used his 
first direct mail ad piece recently 
and it paid off. He says his business 
really picked up the weekend of 
Dec. 7. Heavy snow crippled retail in 
the central Midwest for three days 
after Thanksgiving. 
In Chicago, volume is up. Mont- 
gomery Ward says its stores are up 
29 percent, due to heavy TV adver- 
tising on promo LPs, which help 
create the traffic. Dollars are up but 
units are down at Sears. Chicago re- 
lailen report they are worried about 
early next year, when newspaper ad 
rates go up. 
Discount Records, with three new 
stories, is experiencing a 10 percent 
increase. 
With artists coming out with 
double packages like Elton John's 
"Yellow Brick Road," some of this 
higher priced product is moving 
well, but in general sales remain 
about even with last year. 
"People buy what they want re- 
gardless of price," H.L. Forest, man- 
ager of Rose Discount Records says. 
Andy Anderson, Record Center, 
reports business is up because he is 
getting much catalog business by 
default. He feels labels over -reacted 
by cutting out so many holiday al- 
burnt. 
He points up customers coming in 
after visiting as many au nine stores 
to try to fmd Mitch Miller or Bing 
Crosby LPs. 
Phil Shannon of Stark Record 
Service, N. Canton, Ohio, says his 27 
Camelot stores are even with last 
year. Co-op money wisely spent has 
maintained his business level, he 
says. 
One reason why record retailers 
seem to be doing well this year is be- 
cause of the price of the product. 
Ray Avery, owner of Rare Records 
in Glendale, explains thusly: 
"People do seem to be buying 
records as gifts because of the price. 
We had our best Saturday last week. 
selling a lot of new product and nos- 
talgia." 
Kids are buying the rock LPs 
while their parents are purchasing 
bands (Harry James, Benny Good- 
man, Buddy Rich, Duke Ellington). 
Rare has around 100 small labels in 
stock which offer nostalgic material 
like old radio shows and Ted Lewis 
(on the Sunbeam label).

`Progressive Country' & Soul To Reign? 
Coainned from page J 
buyers picked up on them. Both re- 
flected the musical surroundings of 
the day and drew heavily on major 
artists around them and several im- 
portant predecessors. Both felt a cer- 
tain resistance at first and both sang 
a music that was realistic. 
All of these parallels may be 
found in country music on the whole 
today, 
a particularly "progressive 
country," a category which encom- 
passes a vast number of artists. 
Merle Haggard most certainly be 
considered progressive. He's crossed 
into pop, sings songs that are totally 
realistic (he's been called the work- 
ing man's poet), he's consistently 
been innovative (last year he cut a 
country Dixieland LP), he appeals 
to most audiences and he is known 
to all audiences. 
Kris Kristofferson changed many 
minds about country with songs 
such as "Me and Bobby McGee," 
"Sunday Morning Coming Down," 
"Help Me Make It Through The 
Night" and "Why Me, Lord." Kris - 
toffersoo seemed to have universal 
appeal, saw his songs covered from 
soul to rock to easy listening, but re- 
mained basically country. 
Johnny Cash, with his TV show, 
turned many people into country 
fans without them knowing it. Cash 
sang straight country, protest songs, 
rock and other material. In his early 
days, however, Cash was also con- 
sidered a rebel of sorts. 
Roger Miller turned a lot of heads 
with crossover country, and was re- 
sponsible for the present Grammy 
rule in which a song cannot be nomi- 
nated in more than one category. His 
"King Of The Road" seeps pop and 
country awards in 1965. John Hart- 
ford's "Grade On My Mind" is felt 
by many to be the most progressive 
country songs of the '60s. 
These artists are some of the 
predecessors of the current move- 
ment, and most are still a strong, vi- 
able part of music today. 
So there have been signs of a 
change. Who could be called pro- 
gressive country today? The list is a 
long one. Waylon Jennings, Kristof- 
lesson, Tompall Glaser, Billy Joe 
Shavers, Bobby Bare and to some 
extent 
a Billy Swan or Freddy 
Weller in Nashville. Willie Nelson, 
Kinky Friedman, Jetty Jeff Walker 
and others from Austin fit the pic- 
ture. Others who seem to frs the 
mold, whether straight country or 
not are Ray Wylie Hubbard, Mi- 
chael Murphy, B.W. Stevenson and 
Willie Fong Young. 
Jennings is perhaps the best ex- 
ample of what could happen. For 
the past decade a major country art- 
ist Jennings actually surfaced ago as 
a member of Buddy Holly's band 
some 17 years ago. Over the pas 10 
years he's had major country hits, 
drawn well in concert, but has not 
been considered a truly major star 
until recently. Now, with three con- 
secutive No. I country disks under 
his belt, his latest LP, "Ramblin' 
Man," has started to shoot up the 
pop charts. He's quietly started play- 
ing to audiences in traditional rock 
spots like New York City's Academy 
of Music, and Bottom Line, Wash- 
ington, D.C.'s Cellar Door and Los 
Angeles' Troubadour and Santa 
Monica Civic Auditorium. His ma- 
terial deals with "real" things and 
draws from rock, rockabilly, soul 
and traditional country. Resistance 
to him in the country field is break- 
ing down. 
Willie Nelson has for years writ- 
ten songs covered in all musical 
fields. He's penned pop classics like 
"Funny How Time Slips Away" and 
"Night Life" and country classics 
like "Hello Walls." Now, he's moved 
into spots like the Troubadour. His 
July 4 picnic was nationally tele- 
vised over NBC -TV's rack -oriented 
"Midnight Special." He will be the 
key figure in six upcoming ABC-TV 
shows, working with Shelter- Vision. 
The Specials will include Kinky 
Friedman (whom ABC is launching 
a major pop push with), B.W. Ste- 
venson and Ray Wylie Hubbard. 
Tompall Glaser was one of the 
first artist /businessmen to reach 
Nashville and his studio has become 
a center for many of the artists men- 
tioned above, often produced by 
Ken Mansfield or offered songs by 
Shel Silverstein, both of whom 
learned their crafts in the pop world.

CROWDS AT THE SET 
Beverly Hills Disco 
Is `Elegantly Funky 
LOS ANGELES -The Set, a six - 
month -old soft -rock dance room 
and disco in the high -status Beverly 
Hills district here, has been 
a 
thronged and successful exception 
to this city's coldness towards dance 
clubs in recent years. 
Until the Set opened up, the only 
important record -breaking disco in 
town was Studio One, 
a pre - 
dominently gay room in the cav- 
ernous quarters that formerly 
housed 
the 
private- membership 
Factory. 
Set owners Jim Lavett and Daryll 
Howe spent $200,000 to open up the 
club, doing the job in only 36 days 
from signing the lease. Previously 
four other restaurant or nitery oper- 
ations had failed at the Doheny 
Drive site just south of Wilshire 
Blvd. 
The heart of the Lovett -Howe 
concept is 
a combination of live 
dance music and records in an 
"elegantly funky" environment. 
Says Laves, former executive at the 
Florida -based chain of Big Daddy 
clubs, "We believe that good live 
music alternating with records is 
more exciting than just records all 
the time. It's like the difference be- 
tween going to the stadium to see a 
football game or watching the game 
on television at your neighborhood 
bar." 
In search of a house band, Howe, 
a former pro singer turned success- 
ful interior designer, auditioned 
dozens of groups at a Record Plant 
studio. 
"Every act we heard sounded too 
mechancial, so I wound up assem- 
bling the best of the individual musi- 
cians who came through into a new 
group called the Ivory Brothers. 
They play all the current Top 40 hits, 
but add their own personalities to 
the established hit sound." 
Lavett and Howe now manage 
and publish the Ivory Brothers and 
are getting ready to put together a 
record deal for the group. 
Meanwhile, they are closing the 
arrangements to open another Set in 
the Marina area and have budgeted 
$500,000 to convert a rundown West 
Los Angeles tennis club into an all - 
around entertainment spa with 
dancing and shows as well as com- 
plete health club services for both 
sexes. 
The Set has had Joannie Sommers 
appear and is gingerly experi- 
menting with a policy of nightly 
show sets as well as dancing. The 
owners are hoping to avoid taming 
it into a strictly private club, but 
Beverly Hills municipal ordinances 
about dancing and entertaining 
rooms may force this step in 1975. 
"We're doing what works righ 
now in terms of bringing people in,' 
says Howe, "and I hope we'll al way 
be ready to change our format in or

MARGIE JOSEPH 
"Words (Are Impossible) " -m 
Margie Joseph's Hot 100 debut 
validates Atlantic's claim that she is 
a soul ballad singer in a class with 
Roberta Flack and Aretha. The lush 
swoops of Bacharsch -like melody in 
"Words" are handled 
in elegant 
style by Ms. Joseph, surrounded by 
an Arif Mardin production. 
She is married to her manager, 
Larry McKinley of Colson] in New 
Orleans. A natural -born entertainer 
since childhood in northern Missis- 
sippi, she sang in the usual church 
and school shows before going onto 
Dillard University. Her two Atlantic 
albums are "Margie Joseph" and 
"Sweet Surrender." 
PETER SHELLEY 
"Gee Baby" 90 
Over the past 12 years, Peter Shel- 
ley has established himself as one of 
Britain's leading record producers 
and songwriters. He has a string of 
chart successes to his credit, includ- 
ing all of Alvin Stardust's hits and 
the new hit by Zenda Jacks, "Rub 
My Tummy." His new release "Gee 
Baby," which he also wrote and pro- 
duced, gained a silver disc in Eng- 
land for its popular soft rock feel 
that borders on MOR. 
Magnet Records has released the 
song here under the auspices of 
Arista Records. 
The song starts out in a slow rock 
feel and continues throughout with 
a nice background saxophone riff. 
Listeners will enjoy the song's end- 
ing with free -Bowing background 
vocals by a group of heavenly 
women as Shelley repeats the song's 
title over and over. 
Shelley is accessible through An- 
nie Kenyon of London's Magnet 
Records.

dience of teens and young adults as 
possible with a different format than 
that of the AM station. 
"On the FM, we want the 16 -35 
age listener. with a crunch of 16-24 
age people. With the AM station, we 
want people 18 -49 years of age. 
"The days when a radio station 
could be all things to all people are 
over." 
The FM is pop- oriented in the 
morning and in the evening gets 
more progressive. The playlist here 
includes nine singlet and 20-25 cur- 
rent albume. "We play the best cuts 
from them all. The tenon is that we 
feel people "listen to our FM all day 
long." 
The FM does have impact. 
Recently, on a Sunday, the station 
made one announcement about giv- 
ing away the new George Harrison 
LP at a local record store, Flaming 
Rat Records. The store gave away all 
50 albums within 10 minutes. 
"Next to Detroit, Grand Rapids 
has the highest FM penetration of 
any city in the nation. Here, FM rat- 
ings account for about 62 percent of 
the entire ARB." 
True, a short -list FM station has 
been doing well in ratings in Grand 
Rapids ... "because of the spectrum 
of the market." But Hamilton ex- 
pects to improve consistently in rat- 
ings with the FM and "I don't think 
any tight list is going to hurt our 
AM." 
Not that he takes any chances 
with losing audience on AM. Here. 
though, he has a broader music base. 
The playlist features 35 -38 tunes. 
"We made the AM station broader 
in music appeal because surveys re- 
vealed that music repetition can be a 
tuneout factor. Here, we add two or 
three records a week, depending on 
the product available. Most of the 
new records are played first on the 
FM station, but not necessarily. 
"This is where it really pays for a 
program director to know his market 
and its past history. For instance, 
any record that tells a story-such as 
'The Night The Lights Went Out In 
Georgia'-hits fast here. Or 'Spiders 
And Snakes.' A smart program di- 
rector can use that kind of informa- 
tion to his advantage. 
"Novelty records also do well in 
Grand Rapids. I don't use them as 
power play records. because they 
can turn into negative factors very 
quickly. For example, the 'Earache 
My Eye' record by Cheech & Chong. 
The album was No. 
1 in this market, 
but we had been off the single long, 
long before. Billy "Crash" Craddock 
I'm playing because we're trying to 
grab a more adult audience. 
"Basically, we're looking for 
longer quarter -hour listening on 
AM. 
"I feel, loo, that you have to be 
mom than a jukebox. And we know 
we're successful. If we don't add a 
record on the AM, it won't sell. The 
racks buy from our list ... they know 
our list is valid. 
"What alarms me most is the radio 
stations around that are featuring ly- 
ing lists. 
"They demean all radio." 
SAN DIEGO -"Surprising response" has been the result of announcements 
on the air at XHIS, an FM south -of -the- border station that beams into the 
market, asking listeners to "call as when they cannot find records in the stores 
that they've heard on the station," says program director Bob Gown. 
"We have found that a good portion of the bits receiving play in San Diego 
are unavailable in even the largest record outlets. 
"It's interesting -the record folks are always to anxious to gain airplay for 
new product, but when an item does get local play, your listeners can't even 
buy the damn thing! 
"I think it's time for promotion and distribution to get together. I'd also be 
quite interested to know to what extent this problem exists in other markets."

PAUL ANkA: 
MULTI TALENTEN ARTIST 
SÌNgER,COMpOSER TURNEd SÌNCiER 
ACIAÌN RÌdES THE CREST Of 
NEW -fOUNd populARiTy 
Paul Anka the singer has arrived ...again. 
Although many of the performers of the 
50s era are still familiar names and still work 
regularly, only Anka and Elvis Presley remain 
in the big money as performers. Anka is one 
of the few early rock stars to transcend the 
nostalgia audience and establish himself as a 
major creative force. 
Now Paul Anka is establishing himself as 
the next superstar sex symbol. Paul Anka? 
He is five feet, six inches tall. He has his 
choice of having tailored -made clothes or 
shopping in the Jr.-Hi shop. More than one 
columnist has openly insinuated that there is 
a bald spot there somewhere. Asa singer, he 
works with a limited voice. 
He delivers, he projects style and honesty 
that assault the senses. Wearing a three piece 
tux, he holds his head at a cocky angle, the 
mike cord spread between his two hands and 
takes a strut stance. The lips twitch to accen- 
tuate certain words. He looks great. He's 
worked at it. 
But it's his personality that captures and 
enraptures the women. While Tom Jones, 
Engelbert Humperdinck and Presley have the 
risque jokes, indiscriminately kiss the 
women, not really caring whose napkin they 
use to wipe their face, or around whose neck 
they place a scarf, Anka totally conveys the 
idea that he really cares. You leave the show- 
room positive that the next morning he'd re. 
member your name. He imparts a tenderness 
to women that most male singers don't. And 
it's that tenderness that sets him apart from 
the others. 
It is also that tenderness and sensitivity 
that trademarks an Anka lyric. 
From the frustrations and loneliness of 
youth, to the sadness of lost love to the joys of 
parenthood, Anka captures emotions in gutty 
lyrics, backed by an untrained ability to write 
simple harmony. 
His ability to understand emotions gives 
him the unique ability to go inside another 
artist's soul. 
"My Way," written for Sinatra, describes 
the singer's life so accurately that many fans 
first believed Sinatra penned it. 
The right to remain an individual is impor. 
tant to Anka, as shown in his songs, "I'm Not 
Anyone," and "My Way." In "While We're 
Still Young." Anka's lyrics capture the raw 
emotions of lost love. 
The perception and living in Anka's lyrics can be attributed to his background. 
"Look. when I was 13, 
I was working a strip joint in Canada. My professional training was 
high school hops. In between jobs I worked as a waiter. I collected soup labels and won a con- 
test that sent me on my first trip to New York to see an Alan Freed rock 'n' roll show. The 
second time I came to New York 1 lived in a bathtub and a bongo player friend lent me money 
so 
I could live on coffee and donuts." he relates. 
"When 
I was young I had big dreams and a lack of common sense. 
I had energy and de- 
sire, but I had no idea of what I was doing," he says seriously. "I didn't know if I wanted to be a 
lawyer or be in show business. Writing and recording 'Diana' crystallized my direction. It hap- 
pened very fast." 
He was the youngest performerto headline the Copacabana in New York when he was 19. 
His hits from the 505 reflect the universal timeless emotions of youth. "Puppy Love," 
"You Are My Destiny," "Put Your Head On MyShoulders" -songs that while musically limited, 
nevertheless earned him a popular foundation for a career and $1 million by the time he was 
17. 
He has been through a lot of changes and doesn't dwell on the past, believing in today's 
music. "I believe in change and never put down what is currently happening in music," he 
says. "If you don't change naturally. if you don't adapt, you get caught in a groove and your 
work is quickly eclipsed by other fresher performers." 
He has over 20 million selling records to his credit. His new approach makes you realize 
just how far he has come. His hit "(You're) Having My Baby," mirrors but doesn't copy a simi- 
lar sound of the soul group, The Stylistics, and a much earlier pop group, Paul & Paula. 
His music is still influenced by the earlier rhythm and blues and rock 'n' roll of Chuck 
Berry. Fats Domino and Sonny James. But it has matured, grown up. along with two gener- 
ations of fans. 
Anka has the gift of not only sniffing out trends and following them but also of starting 
them. 
Early recording hits by Anka are going to be reissued. Paul bought back the rights to his 
earlier hits on ABC -Paramount in 1960 for $250,000 because he knew his voice and style were 
changing and he wanted to keep the earlier records off the market. 
However, they became the subject of black market and bootlegging operations, and so he 
has leased the rights back for five years. 
Anka has just made a "$100,000 deal" with Bill Buster of American Record Sales against 
royalities to release many of the old songs on albums. All cuts are from the originals and were 
not redone, though they've been rechanneled for stereo. 
"With the nostalgia thing, we've been getting lots of calls. but until recently we just held 
them back. Original singles of the early things have been getting $50 and $100 apiece," he 
comments. 
In 1971 Gordon Mills bought Anka's Spanka Music for $500,000 in cash and tied Anka up 
for five years, of which a year is left. 
Because of his new hits on United Artists, plus changing management to Alan Carr, Anka 
is now working harder than he has in years. He completed a cross.country sellout concert tour. 
He has extremely lucrative contracts with Harrah's in both Reno and Tahoe, the Fontainebleau 
in Miami Beach and is currently starring at Caesars Palace, Las Vegas. 
Whether in nightclubs or in theaters Anka works alone. "I had to fight to do a one -man 
show. They wanted an opening act. But 
I convinced them all." he stresses. 
"Few places allow a chance for the audience rapport 
I want and need. 
I turn down more 
job offers than 
I take. New York has had it as a nightclub town. You have a better chance of 
being showcased properly in Nevada and a little more freedom," he states. 
Anka takes sound seriously. He endorses Shurr sound equipment, carries and uses Vocal 
Master. When singing at Caesars Palace he uses 12 brass, 30 violins and percussion. 
"Technically the more strings the better." he emphasizes. "You never have enough. With 
less you only hear a technical sound and they tend to press." 
Las Vegas News Bureau photos 
During a year's period he may employ six 
arrangers. He frequently utilizes four arrang. 
ers to put together his nightclub act. He's in 
the habit of giving two arrangers the same 
song. When 'recording he picks the arranger 
for the type of music. 
He has predicted that Nevada hotels will 
eventually get down to one show a night, and 
eliminate the food. At his recent engagement 
at the Fontainebleau, all tables were cleared 
from the room in deference to Anka's prefer. 
ence of being presented "in concert." He also 
personally supervised the complete revision 
of the stage sound system so as to simulate 
the sound of a recording studio. and individ. 
wally miked every instrument in the orches. 
tra. For the first time plexigfass separators 
between band sections were seen on the Fon- 
tainebleau's stage. 
His opinions are definite, but his life has 
changed with the times. 
"The big change in my life came with 'My 
Way,' " he says. "Everything that's happened 
to me, made me write 'My Way.' It crystallized 
as a song for Frank Sinatra. 
"People who didn't realize my credentials 
as a songwriter then discovered that 
I wrote 
the theme music for 'The Longest Day' and 
the theme for 'The Tonight Show.' Johnny's 
theme earns him over $20,000 yearly in royal. 
ities. 
"I trapped myself once," he confesses. "I 
wrote all my hits until as a songwriter I went 
down. After that, if I offered one of my songs 
to another singer, they'd say 'It it's not good 
enough for him, who needs it ?' So 
I decided 
there would be two Paul Ankas." 
"But you've got to separate each career, to 
give respect to the business. Each thing leads 
to something else. The Vegas thing didn't 
happen overnight. 
I had to build a following. 
You have to give up a certain amount of time 
for each thing. You can't all of a sudden go 
heavy rock, that's not what I'm about. It was 
better for me to give away 'She's A Lady' to 
Tom Jones than keep it for myself. A writer 
must respect his song and do what's best for 
it. Otherwise, I'd have too many of them lay- 
ing around, and you can't release them all at 
once. 
"My songwriting commitments now are 
for friends. 
I show them what I'm into and it

Dayton's at present showcases

The uptown store- in addition to an

It's understood that a major mid-

produces unauthorized product 
Another new development is that 
some of the disks are "factory sealed 
for' the customer's protection," 
pressed with quality, colorfully 
packaged and competitively priced, 
from 54.95 to 57.50 for a single al- 
bum. In the early days and until 
recently, the producing and pack- 
aging was far less sophisticated, 
hastily conceived with the pressing 
of poor quality. 
Present -day bootleg companies 
operate generally and basically in 
similar fashion. Recordings come 
from tapes, transcriptions, live per- 
formance or airchecks, or combina- 
tions thereof, without permission of 
the proprietor or from the artists in- 
volved, who were not paid for the 
performance. 
Culled and collated, the record 
appears with a label name, aug- 
mented by an "address" usually a 
Post Office box number, a rather 
vague reference to "protection," or 
some such simile, and a photo of the 
major artist or artists involved. 
In most cases the label is not a sig- 
natory to any agreement with either 
the American Federation of Musi- 
cians or with AFTRA, thus the musi- 
cians or the actors involved haven't 
been paid in accordance with the re- 
quirements of those unions. 
Jazz is the genre that seems to be 
bootlegged the most. (Until recently 
rock concerts by major names 
created a market for unauthorized 
LPs.) Accessibility to jazz product 
has been relatively easy, taken from 
tapes of rehearsals, live perform- 
ances at theaters and hotels, radio 
broadcasts and record sessions. The 
latter. of course, represents those 
gigs never released before on record; 
a fact prominently accented on cov- 
ers by most bootleg labels. 
Jazz is easy game for the unau- 
thorized release, too, because the 
artist has become vulnerable by all 
the exposure on different media, 
therefore making him easy victim to 
these types of recordings. Charlie 
Mingas, for example, claims that he 
has been bootlegged on many al- 
bums because he has performed so 
much. He states that he has never 
given permission nor received any 
royalties for at least two records on 
which he stars. These are on Ozone 
Records album, obtained at Day- 
ton's, "Charlie Mingas- Cecil, Tay- 
lor," consisting of broadcast per- 
formances and a record on Session 
Records, purchased at King Karol, 
entitled, "Hooray For Charlie Min - 
Mingus says "neither of the two 
albums has been approved and I 
have not been paid for anything." A 
check also reveals that both labels 
have never been signatory with the 
AFM. 
Benny Goodman's performances 
abound on bootlegged product. 
When contacted, the Goodman of- 
fice states it is aware of the large 
numbers of unauthorized versions 
available on the market, and is tak- 
ing legal action against several it 
considers bootleggers. 
The once confirms that it has 
never authorized the release of a

Black people's listening has not 
changed very much over the years, 
nor their need to get involved with 
the holiday spirit. The black deejays 
might involve themselves in putting 
forth that spirit (even with all the 
bad times in the world) by bringing 
a little soul into the season (and es- 
pecially during this week). 
They might start by digging out 
some of the old classics catching dust 
in the station's library. They'll prob- 
ably be surprised by what's there; 
like a few gems from Lou Rawls, 
James Brown, Kenny Burrell, the 
Jackson 5, Ramsey Lewis, and, of 
course, the evergreen by Nat Cole. 
Let's get some soul into Christ- 
mas.
